ABSTRACT: Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is an immunologically mediated
central nervous system disorder that is infrequently associated with malig-
nancy. We report a 31-year-old woman who developed SPS after autolo-
gous bone marrow transplantation and subsequent interferon treatment for
multiple myeloma. Anti– glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD) antibody
serology was positive. The myeloma remains in remission 10 years post-
transplant. SPS has been described in association with lung cancer and
breast cancer, thymoma, and Hodgkin lymphoma. This is the second report
of SPS in a patient with myeloma and the ﬁrst description of SPS following
autologous transplantation. Aberrant immune reconstitution is known to
occur following hematopoietic progenitor cell transplantation. Interferon is
also known to augment the immune response posttransplant. We speculate
that an aberrant posttransplant immune response may have caused both the
SPS and an autologous graft-versus-myeloma effect, resulting in prolonged
remission posttransplant.

CASE REPORT
A 31-year-old woman developed severe back pain in
1995. A sacral plasmacytoma was found and was
treated with external beam radiation (4500 cGy in 25
fractions). Over the following 2 years, bone marrow
plasmacytosis developed, and the diagnosis of IgG-
kappa multiple myeloma was made in December
1997. Multiple lytic lesions were found throughout
her skeleton. In 1998, the patient underwent an
autologous bone marrow transplant following condi-

tioning with total body irradiation (1200 cGy in six

fractions) and intravenous melphalan (140 mg/m 2).
Subsequently, she received maintenance interferon
A, 10,000,000 units subcutaneously three times a
week for several years. She remains in an excellent
remission 10 years following the transplant with a
stable sacral bony lesion as the only residual mani-
festation of her disease.
During the ﬁrst 2 years posttransplant, the pa-
tient developed muscular discomfort and spasms in
her right hip. These spread to her legs, abdomen,
neck, shoulders, and toes over several months. Pre-
cipitants of the spasms included stress, emotional
upset, fatigue, and walking. The patient complained
of weakness and difﬁculty walking. In addition, she
developed myoclonic jerks (approximately 100 per
day) involving her trunk. The myoclonus was largely
eliminated with oral baclofen, 20 mg three times
daily.
Her past medical history was notable for scoliosis,
hypothyroidism, and chronic hepatitis C. She was
not diabetic and had no personal or family history of
other endocrine or neurological disease.
On examination, in March 2003, the patient’s
cranial nerves were normal. Tone was mildly in-
creased in her legs. Strength was normal. She was
hyperreﬂexic except at the ankles, where reﬂexes
could not be elicited. Plantar stimulation evoked
strong withdrawal, without a classical Babinski sign.
Sensation was normal. Cerebellar testing was normal
except slight end-point dysmetria in the right arm.
Her gait was wide-based, slow, and stiff, and she
preferred to use a cane. There was lumbar hyperlor-
dosis, thoracic kyphosis, and thoracolumbar scolio-
sis.
Electromyography revealed continuous motor
unit potential activity with superimposed spasms in
the legs more than the arms. There was no evidence
of myopathy or peripheral neuropathy.
Antibody testing revealed markedly increased se-
rum anti–GAD 65 antibody titer at 104 nmol/L (nor-
mal /H110210.02 nmol/L). Amphiphysin, anti-neuronal
antibody types 1 (anti-Hu) and 2 (anti-Ri), Purkinje
cell cytoplasmic antibody types 1 and 2, and N- and
P/Q-type calcium-channel antibody serologies were
negative. Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies were nega-
tive; thyrotropin-binding antibodies were in the bor-
derline range at 1.1 U/L (normal /H110211.0 U/L, ele-
vated /H110222.0 U/L). Serum creatine kinase was
minimally elevated at 132 U/L (normal 15–120
U/L). Low-resolution HLA typing revealed DRB1
03, 07, and DQB1 02 (homozygous). Magnetic reso-
nance imaging of the spine showed thoracolumbar
scoliosis but no spinal cord compression or abnor-
mal cord signal. Computed tomography of the head
was normal. Cerebrospinal ﬂuid was not examined.
Treatment for SPS began in April 2003. the pa-
tient initially received 1 g/kg intravenous immuno-
globulin (IVIg) on 2 consecutive days, given monthly
for 4 months. This substantially improved her
spasms, balance, and gait. Her symptoms recurred
during the 3 months following IVIg treatment. A
second course of IVIg (1 g/kg) on 2 consecutive days
monthly was administered beginning in November
2003. This resulted in a less dramatic improvement.
An 8-week course of weekly intravenous methylpred-
nisone (250 mg) may have resulted in a small addi-
tional improvement. Diazepam was prescribed for
nighttime waking due to stiffness and myoclonic
jerks; this provided minimal relief and was subse-
quently discontinued. Since May 2004, she has re-
ceived ongoing IVIg treatment (1 g/kg on 2 consec-
utive days per month). With this treatment, her

overall level of function has been good, but some
truncal stiffness and gait impairment persists. Her
nighttime spasms have gradually decreased in sever-
ity. This treatment regimen continues to the present.
On annual follow-up, no clinical, laboratory or ra-
diological evidence of recurrent myeloma has been
found.

Our patient did not re -
ceive thalidomide treatment. She did, however, re-
ceive a prolonged course of interferon. Interferon

can augment the immune response and may have
contributed to the development of SPS.
We cannot exclude the possibility that SPS devel-
oped independently of both the BMT and the my-
eloma. However, in both our patient and the patient
reported by Schiff et al., SPS appeared within 5 years
following the presentation of myeloma. The sequen-
tial occurrence of these two rare diseases within a few
years is unlikely to occur by chance.
In conclusion, we have described a patient who
presented initially with an osseous plasmacytoma
and subsequently developed multiple myeloma. She
went on to develop SPS following treatment, which
included an autologous hematopoietic cell trans-
plant. Although her myeloma remains in remission
since the transplant, SPS persists. In view of her
prolonged remission following autologous trans-
plant, we speculate that the autoimmune process
that developed may be an immunologic effect con-
tributing to the persistent remission. In the context
of aberrant immune reconstitution, which occurs
following autologous hematopoietic cell transplanta-
tion, the SPS in this patient may represent an autol-
ogous graft-versus-myeloma phenomenon.
